questions.model_answer:
a) Infant botulism (intestinal colonization by Clostridium botulinum with in situ toxin production; ages 6 days to 12 months present with constipation followed by feeding difficulty, hypotonia, weak cry, descending paralysis, and airway compromise).
b) Send stool (feces) for demonstration of botulinum toxin and/or toxin-producing organism, plus serum for toxin; the traditional gold-standard test is the mouse bioassay (neutralization with type-specific antitoxin to identify toxin type).
c) (1) Human botulinum immune globulin (BabyBIG) 50 mg/kg IV, given as early as possible (greatest benefit within the first 3 days of hospitalization; reduces length of mechanical ventilation, ICU stay, and total hospital stay). (2) Avoid aminoglycosides and tetracyclines, which impair neuronal calcium entry and worsen botulism. HBAT (equine heptavalent antitoxin) is NOT approved for infants younger than 1 year.

cohort_answer.text: Diagnosis: Infant botulism. Sample: Serum, stool. Test: Toxin neutralization bioassay in mice to detect botulinum toxin in serum, stool, enema fluid, gastric aspirate, or suspect foods, OR enriched selective media to isolate from stool/foods. Treatment: Human derived antitoxin (Human Botulism Immune Globulin) - significantly decreases days of mechanical ventilation, ICU stay, and total hospital stay by almost 1 month. Avoid aminoglycosides - will worsen paralysis. Equine derived heptavalent botulinum antitoxin for adult/peds botulism. Caution: delay routine live-virus vaccines for 6 months after receipt of BabyBIG.

questions.model_answer: (1) Foodborne botulism (ingestion of preformed toxin). (2) Wound botulism (spores introduced into a wound germinate and produce toxin). (3) Inhalational botulism (toxin crosses the pulmonary alveolar epithelium; e.g., bioterrorism or contaminated cocaine). [Adult intestinal colonization botulism of unknown etiology is a further recognized form.]

questions.model_answer: Conventional diagnosis relies on demonstrating toxin in serum, gastric secretions, stool, or food samples. The most sensitive traditional method is the mouse bioassay: sample is injected into mice, which are observed for botulism symptoms; toxin type is determined by protecting a parallel group with type-specific antitoxin. Anaerobic cultures of serum, stool, and implicated food may assist but rarely yield the organism.

questions.model_answer: Demonstration of botulinum toxin or toxin-producing C. botulinum in the feces, and/or detection of toxin in serum. Because infant botulism results from intestinal colonization with in situ toxin production, stool is the highest-yield specimen; toxin/organism excretion may continue for up to 1 month.

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Foodborne botulism (ingested preformed toxin). (2) Wound botulism (spores germinate in a wound). (3) Inhalational botulism (toxin absorbed across alveolar epithelium). [Adult intestinal colonization botulism is a further form.]

questions.model_answer: Three routes (excluding infant): (1) foodborne (ingested preformed toxin); (2) wound (spores germinate in a wound); (3) inhalational (toxin crosses alveolar epithelium). Adjunctive specific therapy: botulinum antitoxin given as early as possible - heptavalent botulinum antitoxin (HBAT, equine) for patients 1 year and older (BabyBIG for infants). Additional specific therapy for one situation: in wound botulism, perform debridement (with anaerobic cultures at surgery) and give penicillin G 10-20 million units/day (metronidazole as alternative).

questions.model_answer: (1) Foodborne botulism - preformed toxin ingested with food, absorbed in the duodenum/jejunum, reaching peripheral cholinergic synapses. (2) Wound botulism - spores introduced into a wound germinate and produce toxin. (3) Inhalational botulism - toxin crosses the pulmonary alveolar epithelium into the bloodstream. [Note: the part as printed asks for ways of acquiring infant botulism; infant/adult colonization botulism occurs via ingestion of spores that germinate in the gut and produce toxin in situ.]

cohort_answer.text: Infant botulism – ingestion of spores that germinate in infant's intestines and produce toxin, from home-canned vegetables, fruits, fish, honey. Foodborne botulism – preformed toxin ingested with food, absorbed in small intestine, reaches peripheral cholinergic synapses. Wound botulism – spores introduced into a wound where they germinate and produce toxin. Inhalational botulism – toxin absorbed through alveolar epithelium into bloodstream (speaker notes: contaminated food e.g. honey)

questions.model_answer:
a) Infant botulism.
b) Mouse bioassay demonstrating botulinum toxin (toxin neutralized by type-specific antitoxin); stool/enema and serum are the specimens, with toxin detectable and stool cultures positive for up to ~1 month.
c) (1) Human botulinum immune globulin (BabyBIG), which reduces length of ICU stay, duration of mechanical ventilation, and overall hospital stay, greatest benefit within the first 3 days of hospitalization. (2) Avoid aminoglycosides (and other antibiotics acting in the gut), as aminoglycosides impair neuronal calcium entry and worsen botulism, and antibiotic-induced lysis of C. botulinum in the gut can increase available toxin.
d) Ingested spores (from soil-contaminated environmental sources; formerly honey) colonize the infant intestine because the immature microbiota is permissive for germination; C. botulinum produces neurotoxin in situ, which is absorbed into the bloodstream, reaches peripheral cholinergic synapses/neuromuscular junction, and prevents release of acetylcholine, producing flaccid paralysis.

cohort_answer.text:
Botulism (typically <6 months, descending paralysis preceded by constipation). Ddx: acute flaccid paralysis from poliovirus, enterovirus, WNV, GBS, rabies
Botulinum toxin neutralization bioassay in mice; isolate toxin from serum/stool(highest yield)/enema fluid/gastric aspirate/suspect foods (often negative in infant); isolation of spores in food; EMG (non-specific)
BabyBIG (reduces ICU LOS, ventilation, hospitalization days); avoid antimicrobials (risk of lysis of intraluminal C. botulinum increasing toxin absorption, AG can potentiate neurotoxin)
Absorption of botulinum toxin into circulation from mucosa (toxin A and B important). Results from ingested spores which germinate/multiply/produce toxin in large gut via colonization. Neurotoxin blocks cholinergic neuromuscular innervation by preventing neurotransmitter release

questions.model_answer: a) Wound botulism. Spores contaminate the wound, germinate, and produce toxin; the incubation period is ~4 to 14 days. It lacks the gastrointestinal prodrome of foodborne botulism but otherwise presents with symmetrical descending cranial neuropathies and bulbar/respiratory failure; the wound may appear to be healing well while neurologic manifestations progress.

questions.model_answer:
a) Mouse bioassay (neutralization bioassay) - traditionally the most sensitive means of botulinum toxin detection.
b) (1) Serum; (2) Stool; (3) Gastric secretions; (4) Suspected/implicated food. (Wound tissue/anaerobic wound culture in wound botulism.)
c) (1) Foodborne (ingestion of preformed toxin); (2) Wound (spores introduced into a wound, e.g., black-tar heroin injection); (3) Inhalational (toxin crosses pulmonary alveolar epithelium; e.g., contaminated cocaine or bioterrorism). [Iatrogenic cosmetic/therapeutic use and adult intestinal colonization are additional routes.]
d) Heptavalent botulinum antitoxin (HBAT), the equine antitoxin to toxin types A-G, is the specific therapy for non-infant botulism, most effective within 2 days of symptom onset. For infant (<1 year) botulism, human botulinum immune globulin (BabyBIG) is used instead (HBAT is not approved in infants).

cohort_answer.text: Gold standard: Mouse bioassay - neurotoxin detection. Specimens: Serum; Stool; gastric fluid; Wound (debrided tissue or anaerobic culture); Food suspected as source. Other routes: Wounds; Foodborne; Iatrogenic - cosmetic. Specific therapy: Botulinum antitoxin (BAT); Human derived botulism immune globulin - for infant botulism
